title: The Climax & Resolution
description: The homophobic attack, Adam's hospitalisation, and the road to recovery and reconciliation.
content_html:
The Evening of the Attack

The novel's most violent and pivotal sequence takes place at a party following a celebration at the Bar Belle pub — an event connected to Dante's eighteenth birthday. The two storylines that have been running in parallel throughout the novel — Dante's fatherhood and Adam's secret relationship — are brought together at this party. Adam is present. Josh is present. Logan and Paul are present. The scene is set for a catastrophic collision.

Earlier in the evening, Adam is outed in front of the group. This exposure is the trigger for what follows. The information lands badly in this environment — a social world built on masculine conformity, where homophobia has been casual and unchallenged.

The Attackers: Josh, Logan, and Paul

The attack on Adam is carried out by three people: Josh, Logan, and Paul. All three are Dante's friends. This fact — that Adam's attackers are people Dante has trusted — is central to the novel's emotional and thematic force.

The specific roles are equally important. Josh — Adam's own secret boyfriend — is the one who beats Adam. Logan and Paul physically restrain Dante, preventing him from intervening. Josh does not stand back. He does not hesitate. He attacks the person he has been intimate with.

Key Fact

The attackers are Josh, Logan, and Paul — all Dante's friends. Josh, Adam's former secret boyfriend, is the one who beats Adam. Logan and Paul hold Dante back. The attack is a direct product of internalised homophobia: Josh attacks the person he has been with in order to prove, to Logan and to himself, that he is not gay.

Logan's Engineering: A Test of Masculinity

The attack is not spontaneous. It is later revealed that Logan engineered the situation as a test. Logan knows — or suspects — that Josh has been involved with Adam. He uses the moment of Adam being outed to corner Josh: prove you are not gay, or be outed yourself. The logic of the test is the logic of peer pressure taken to its most violent extreme.

Josh does not resist. He is not strong enough — not yet — to withstand the pressure. He chooses violence over vulnerability. In attacking Adam, he attacks the version of himself he cannot accept. Blackman makes this psychologically coherent: Josh's violence is the product of shame, not of hatred in its simplest form. He is not a monster. He is a person who has been broken by the social world he lives in — and who, in his breaking, breaks someone else catastrophically.

The fact that Adam's attacker is his own boyfriend — the person who, in a different world, should be his protector — is the novel's most powerful irony. Blackman constructs this carefully. Josh and Adam's relationship has been built on secrecy and Josh's shame. The attack is the logical endpoint of that shame: Josh, given a social test, chooses violence over honesty. The relationship that Adam hoped might contain connection instead contains the instrument of his hospitalisation. This is what internalised homophobia destroys.

Adam Hospitalised

The attack leaves Adam in critical condition. He is not taken home. He does not recover at the kitchen table. Adam is hospitalised. The severity of the attack is conveyed through the gravity of his medical status: this was not a scuffle. This was a serious, sustained assault.

Dante, after being restrained and unable to stop the attack, reports to the police what happened. He names the attackers. This is an act of moral clarity in a moment of devastation: Dante does not protect his friends by staying silent. He tells the truth — which is, perhaps, the closest he comes in this moment to the journalist he planned to be.

Key Fact

Adam is hospitalised in critical condition. Dante reports to the police what happened and names the attackers. Adam does not go home after the attack. His recovery takes place after his hospitalisation, during which he withdraws, becomes depressed, and eventually faces a suicidal crisis before recovering.

Adam's Recovery: Depression and Withdrawal

After his discharge from hospital, Adam withdraws. He does not bounce back. He stays in his room. He barely communicates. He becomes depressed. The novel does not skip from the attack to recovery. It insists on the reality that violence of this kind has lasting consequences. Adam's mental health deteriorates to the point of a suicidal crisis.

Blackman handles this section with considerable care. Adam's depression is not presented as weakness. It is a rational response to being severely beaten by someone he trusted, in a public setting, while the people he might have looked to for protection were unable to help him. His withdrawal is a form of protection, a body and mind recoiling from a world that has shown itself to be dangerous.

Blackman's choice to show Adam's depression and withdrawal in full is part of the novel's commitment to honesty. A version of this story could have shown Adam attacked and then resilient — a triumph-over-adversity narrative. Instead, Blackman insists on the full cost: hospitalisation, depression, withdrawal, suicidal ideation. This is the real shape of trauma recovery. It is also part of the novel's argument: the violence is not just a bad night. It has consequences that last.

Josh's Confession and Accountability

Eventually, Josh's own story catches up with him. He kisses Dante — revealing to Dante that he is gay himself. He apologises to Adam, unreservedly. And he turns himself in to the police. This does not undo what he did. It does not restore what was taken from Adam. But it is the closest the novel comes to showing the human capacity for accountability among those who have caused harm.

Josh's arc is a tragedy of internalised homophobia: a person who had the capacity for love but was destroyed by shame, who destroyed someone else before finding the courage to be honest. His eventual honesty is not redemption in the full sense — Blackman is too precise for that — but it is an acknowledgement of truth.

Resolution: Resilience and Acceptance

The novel's resolution refuses simple happiness. Adam recovers — physically and, over time, emotionally. He does not become the person he was before the attack. But he survives. Dante, in parallel, has grown into his relationship with Mel. The family, including Tyler, has been brought to a point of greater openness. The reconciliation is hard-won and real.

Blackman ends the novel with Dante embracing fatherhood rather than enduring it, and Adam facing a future rather than being defined by his ordeal. Neither resolution is easy or uncomplicated. But both are earned — through suffering, growth, and the particular resilience that the novel argues is available to people who refuse to let shame govern their lives.
exam_tip_html: The climax is the most heavily examined part of the novel for Edexcel. Make sure you can name all three attackers (Josh, Logan, Paul) and explain their specific roles. Be explicit that Josh beats Adam — his role as Adam's former boyfriend makes this the novel's central irony. And be precise about Adam's aftermath: he is hospitalised in critical condition, then withdraws into depression before recovering. Examiners reward precision about sequence and consequence.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The attackers are Josh, Logan, and Paul — all Dante's friends. Josh beats Adam; Logan and Paul restrain Dante. The attack is engineered by Logan as a test of Josh's masculinity.
  • Josh is Adam's former secret boyfriend — his decision to beat Adam is the product of internalised homophobia and shame, not simple hatred.
  • Adam is hospitalised in critical condition. Dante reports to the police and names the attackers. Adam does not go home after the attack.
  • Adam withdraws into depression and faces a suicidal crisis before recovering. Blackman refuses to fast-forward to resilience — she insists on the full cost of the violence.
  • Josh eventually confesses, apologises to Adam, and turns himself in to the police — accountability, not redemption.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present the homophobic attack and its aftermath as the central crisis of the novel? You should consider the context in which the novel was written.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of the attack as a structural and thematic climax. Discusses: the engineering by Logan, Josh's role as Adam's former boyfriend, Adam's hospitalisation, Dante's report to police, Adam's depression and suicidal crisis. Context: homophobic violence in early 21st-century Britain, Blackman's refusal to soften the aftermath. Comments on the novel's structural convergence of the two storylines.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Blackman uses Josh's participation in the attack to develop the theme of internalised homophobia.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive thematic analysis. Discusses: Josh as Adam's secret boyfriend and his attacker — the central irony; Logan's engineering of the attack as a test; Josh's choice of violence over vulnerability; his eventual confession and turn-in to police. Context: peer pressure, masculinity, shame. Blackman's argument that internalised homophobia destroys the person who carries it as well as the person it targets.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: "Blackman refuses to allow the reader an easy recovery narrative." How does the novel's treatment of Adam's aftermath support this view?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive discussion of narrative honesty. Discusses: hospitalisation, depression, withdrawal, suicidal ideation — the full arc of trauma rather than a shortcut to resilience. How this choice deepens the novel's moral seriousness. Blackman's refusal to sentimentalise or minimise the consequences of violence. Context: mental health, the long effects of hate crime.
Top band (16-20): Clear argument.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant discussion.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present Dante's response to the attack, and what does his behaviour reveal about his character?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of Dante's moral choices. Discusses: physical restraint preventing him intervening; reporting to police and naming his friends as attackers; the parallel with journalism — Dante tells the truth at great personal cost. His protectiveness towards Adam as evidence of the growth he has undergone through fatherhood. His decision to report as moral clarity.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman use the resolution of the novel to suggest that resilience is possible but hard-won?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of resolution. Discusses: Adam's recovery as slow, not triumphant; Dante embracing rather than enduring fatherhood; the family's movement towards greater openness; Josh's accountability as partial acknowledgement. The novel's refusal of easy happiness alongside its insistence that survival is possible. Context: resilience, recovery, the possibility of change.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Blackman presents peer pressure as a force that shapes male behaviour in the novel.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive contextual analysis. Discusses: Logan engineering the attack as a test; Josh unable to resist peer pressure even when it requires violence against someone he cares about; the social world of Dante's friend group as one in which homophobia is tolerated and even weaponised. Context: masculinity norms, group identity, moral courage under social pressure. Blackman's argument that silence and complicity are forms of participation.

knowledge_checks.q: Who are the three attackers in the novel's climactic assault?
What is Josh's specific role in the attack?
options: Josh beats Adam while Logan and Paul restrain Dante
Josh holds Dante while Logan attacks Adam
Josh tries to stop the attack but is overpowered
Josh is not present — he only hears about it afterwards

knowledge_checks.q: What happens to Adam immediately after the attack? (Complete the answer: _____)
options: Dante takes him home and comforts him
Adam is treated at the scene and goes to the police station
Adam is hospitalised in critical condition

knowledge_checks.q: Logan engineers the attack as a _____ — forcing Josh to prove he is not gay.
options: plan to get rid of Dante's friends

knowledge_checks.q: Match each event to its correct place in the sequence:
left: Josh turns himself in to the police
right: Triggers the conditions for the attack
The immediate consequence of Josh, Logan, and Paul's assault
Josh's eventual act of accountability after confessing to Dante

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three attackers and their specific roles.
flashcard_questions.a: Josh beats Adam. Logan and Paul restrain Dante. All three are Dante's friends.
Logan engineers the attack as a test — Josh must prove he is not gay. Josh's internalised homophobia means he chooses violence over vulnerability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the relationship between Josh and Adam before the attack?
flashcard_questions.a: Josh is Adam's secret boyfriend — a closeted, ashamed relationship conducted entirely in secret at Josh's insistence.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to Adam immediately after the attack?
flashcard_questions.a: He is hospitalised in critical condition. Dante reports to the police and names the attackers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Adam's psychological condition after the attack?
flashcard_questions.a: He withdraws, becomes depressed, and faces a suicidal crisis before eventually recovering.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Josh do in the novel's later stages?
flashcard_questions.a: He kisses Dante (revealing his own sexuality), apologises unreservedly to Adam, and turns himself in to the police.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Josh's role as Adam's attacker the novel's central irony?
flashcard_questions.a: Josh was Adam's secret boyfriend — the person who should have been his protector became the instrument of the worst harm done to him.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Dante's decision to report to the police reveal about his character?
flashcard_questions.a: Moral clarity — he tells the truth and names his own friends as attackers, at great personal cost.

glossary_terms.definition: Having one's sexual orientation revealed publicly without consent. Adam is outed at the party, triggering the conditions for the attack.
A medical term indicating a patient's condition is severe and potentially life-threatening. Adam is hospitalised in critical condition after the attack.
The acceptance of negative social attitudes about one's own sexual orientation. Josh's internalised homophobia drives him to attack the person he has been intimate with.
Social pressure to conform to group behaviour and expectations. Logan exploits peer pressure to engineer Josh's attack on Adam.
Taking moral responsibility for harmful actions and submitting to the consequences. Josh's turn-in to the police is an act of accountability.
